questions.question: Why is outline:none a common accessibility failure?
questions.answer: It removes the only visible indication of keyboard focus, making navigation impossible for keyboard and switch users. Replace it with a visible custom focus style, typically via :focus-visible.

questions.question: What contrast ratios does WCAG AA require?
questions.answer: 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (≥24px, or ≥18.66px bold). UI component boundaries and focus indicators also need 3:1.

questions.question: When should you use display:none versus sr-only?
questions.answer: display:none when content is irrelevant to everyone and should be removed from layout and assistive tech. sr-only when content is meant for screen readers but not visually shown, such as labels or hints.

questions.question: What does prefers-reduced-motion require from CSS?
questions.answer: Disable or shorten non-essential animations/transitions, avoid large or infinite motion, and turn off smooth scrolling. Essential state changes should still occur instantly.

questions.question: Why are logical properties an accessibility/RTL concern?
questions.answer: They express spacing and borders in inline/block terms that follow writing direction, so RTL and vertical writing modes lay out correctly without separate physical left/right overrides.

questions.question: Create a visible focus ring for all interactive elements.
Why is text over a photo hard to keep accessible?
questions.answer: Contrast varies across the image, so parts of the text may fall below 4.5:1. Use a consistent overlay/panel and check the worst-case region, not the average.

questions.question: Why is forced-color-adjust:none risky?
questions.answer: It opts the element out of the user's forced-colors palette, potentially making text or borders invisible. Reserve it for cases where author colors are essential and verify contrast manually.
